_schema: Room content. The renderer's trust boundary, enforced in room.js:
_plain: PLAIN TEXT, escaped on render: cards[].name, groups[].title, groups[].symbols[].n
_raw: RAW AUTHORED HTML, injected as-is: cards[].body, cards[].note, examples[].q, examples[].steps[], examples[].ans, groups[].symbols[].g
_rule: Anything moved between those two lists changes what the browser does with it. Plain fields must never contain markup; raw fields are trusted and must never hold anything a reader typed.

cards.name: What the table is ordered by
cards.body: Elements run in order of atomic number Z — the number of protons — left to right, top to bottom.
cards.note: Not by mass. Mendeleev ordered by mass and had to swap a few pairs to make the families line up; Moseley showed in 1913 that Z was the real ordering, and the swaps stopped being exceptions. Te (127.6) still sits before I (126.9).

cards.name: Periods and groups
cards.body:
A period is a row — the highest occupied energy level, n.
A group is a column — elements with the same valence electron count, and so the same chemistry.
cards.note: A group is a family: everything in group 1 is a soft metal that forms a +1 ion, in every period. This is the whole point of the table.

cards.name: Atomic structure from a tile
cards.body:
Z = protons = electrons in a neutral atom.
Neutrons = mass number − Z.
The atomic mass on the tile is the weighted average over the element's natural isotopes.
cards.note: Z identifies the element and never changes. Change the neutrons and you have an isotope; change the electrons and you have an ion.

cards.name: Why atomic masses are not whole numbers
cards.body:
Chlorine is 35.45 because natural chlorine is about 75.8% 35Cl and 24.2% 37Cl.
average = Σ (fraction × isotope mass)
cards.note: A mass in brackets — Tc is [98] — means the element has no stable isotope at all, so the figure is the longest-lived one instead of an average.

cards.name: Valence electrons from the group
cards.body:
Groups 1 and 2: valence = the group number.
Groups 13–18: valence = group number − 10.
cards.note: The single most useful shortcut on the page. Carbon is group 14, so 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons — which is why it makes four bonds and why organic chemistry exists.

cards.name: Reading an electron configuration
cards.body:
Fill in order of energy, write in order of shell:
Cl (Z = 17) = 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5
Shorthand: [Ne] 3s2 3p5
cards.note: The superscripts must add up to Z. That is your check, every time.

cards.name: Blocks: s, p, d, f
cards.body: Groups 1–2 fill an s subshell, groups 13–18 a p, the transition metals a d, the two detached rows an f.
cards.note: The table's odd shape is just the subshell capacities drawn out: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14. Count the columns in each block.

cards.name: Effective nuclear charge
cards.body:
Zeff = the pull an outer electron actually feels, after the inner electrons screen it.
Across a period Zeff rises. Down a group the outer shell is further out and better screened.
cards.note: Learn this one and you get every trend below for free — radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity are all this one idea seen from different sides.

cards.name: Atomic radius
cards.body:
Across a period → radius falls (more protons, same shell, pulled tighter).
Down a group ↓ radius grows (a whole new shell).
cards.note: Across beats down for surprise value: Na is 166 pm and Cl is 102 pm, in the same row. Shade the table by Atomic radius to see it.

cards.name: Ionisation energy
cards.body:
The energy to strip one electron off a gaseous atom.
Across → it rises. Down ↓ it falls.
cards.note: Exactly opposite to radius, and for the same reason: the closer and more tightly held the electron, the more it costs to remove.

cards.name: Two dips that are not mistakes
cards.body:
B (800.6) is below Be (899.5) — the new electron starts a p subshell, higher in energy.
O (1313.9) is below N (1402.3) — oxygen's fourth p electron must pair up, and paired electrons repel.
cards.note: Courses love asking about these two. The trend is a slope, not a staircase.

cards.name: Successive ionisation energies
cards.body:
Mg: 738 → 1451 → 7733 kJ/mol.
The jump between the 2nd and 3rd shows magnesium has exactly two valence electrons.
cards.note: A huge jump means you have started breaking into the noble-gas core. Count the electrons before the jump and you have the group.

cards.name: Electronegativity
cards.body: How hard an atom pulls on the electrons in a bond it is already in. Pauling scale, F = 3.98 at the top, Cs and Fr = 0.79 at the bottom.
cards.note: Rises across, falls down — the top right corner (minus the noble gases) is the greedy corner. He, Ne and Ar have no Pauling value at all; they had no known compounds to measure.

cards.name: Using electronegativity difference
cards.body:
ΔEN < 0.4 — nonpolar covalent
0.4 to 1.7 — polar covalent
> 1.7 — ionic
cards.note: Rough cutoffs, not laws — the boundary is a gradient. But they will get you the right answer on a general-chemistry exam.

cards.name: Ionic radius
cards.body:
A cation is smaller than its parent atom — it usually loses its whole outer shell.
An anion is larger — the same nuclear charge is now spread over more electrons.
Ionic radii: Na+ 102 pm, Mg2+ 72 pm, F− 133 pm, Cl− 181 pm.
cards.note: Atom-to-ion comparisons are directional, not arithmetic: the atom figure and the ion figure come from different definitions of “radius” and are not measured the same way. Within one definition the ordering always holds. For an isoelectronic series (same electron count) radius simply falls as Z rises: N<sup>3−</sup> > O<sup>2−</sup> > F<sup>−</sup> > Na<sup>+</sup> > Mg<sup>2+</sup> > Al<sup>3+</sup>.

cards.name: Oxidation states you can predict
cards.body:
Group 1 → +1, group 2 → +2, group 13 → +3.
Group 15 → −3, group 16 → −2, group 17 → −1, group 18 → 0.
cards.note: Main-group elements go to the nearest noble-gas configuration. Transition metals have several available states — that is why they need a Roman numeral in the name.

cards.name: Metals, metalloids, nonmetals
cards.body: The staircase from B down to At splits them. Metals (left) lose electrons and conduct. Nonmetals (right) gain or share them. Metalloids sit on the line and do both — B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te.
cards.note: Metal + nonmetal usually gives an ionic compound; nonmetal + nonmetal gives a covalent one. Filter by category in the legend to see the blocks.

cards.name: The families worth knowing by name
cards.body:
Group 1 alkali metals — soft, violently reactive, +1.
Group 2 alkaline earth — +2.
Group 17 halogens — reactive nonmetals, −1.
Group 18 noble gases — full shell, nearly inert.
cards.note: Reactivity runs opposite ways at the two edges: down group 1 it increases (the electron is easier to lose), down group 17 it decreases (harder to attract one).

cards.name: Which elements life uses
cards.body: C, H, O, N, P, S build the molecules. Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup> carry the charge and the signals. Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, Se, I, Co, Mo run the enzymes.
cards.note: About 99% of your mass is just O, C, H, N, Ca and P. Click any element for the biology and bench notes on its card.

cards.name: Where the table shows up on the bench
cards.body:
Flame tests read group 1 and 2 by colour — Na yellow, K lilac, Ca orange-red.
Isotopes are the label: 14C dating, 32P and 125I tracers, 2H and 13C in NMR.
cards.note: Molar mass for every stoichiometry calculation you will ever do comes off this table. Search a symbol above to get it.

examples.q: How many valence electrons does phosphorus have, and what ion does it form?
steps: P is group 15
Valence = 15 − 10 = 5
It needs 3 more to reach 8, so it gains 3

examples.q: Write the electron configuration of iron (Z = 26)
steps: Nearest smaller noble gas is Ar (Z = 18), so start [Ar]
26 − 18 = 8 electrons left to place
Fill 4s before 3d, but write by shell: 3d before 4s

examples.q: Rank by atomic radius: Mg, Ca, S
steps: Mg and S are both period 3 — across a period radius falls, so Mg > S
Ca is directly below Mg — down a group radius grows, so Ca > Mg

examples.q: Which has the higher first ionisation energy, nitrogen or oxygen?
steps: The trend across a period says oxygen — it is further right
But O must pair a fourth electron in its 2p subshell, and that repulsion makes it easier to remove
Measured: N = 1402 kJ/mol, O = 1314 kJ/mol
examples.ans: Nitrogen — one of the two dips in the trend

examples.q: An element's ionisation energies are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577 kJ/mol. Which group is it in?
steps: Find the big jump: between the 3rd and 4th (2745 → 11 577)
So 3 electrons come off easily, then the core resists
3 valence electrons ⇒ group 13

examples.q: Is the H–Cl bond ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar?
examples.ans: Polar covalent — shared, but pulled toward Cl

examples.q: Rank the isoelectronic ions by radius: Na⁺, F⁻, Mg²⁺, O²⁻
steps: All four have 10 electrons, so only the nuclear charge differs
More protons pulling the same 10 electrons ⇒ smaller ion

examples.q: Why is caesium the most reactive metal on the table?
steps: Group 1, so one valence electron to lose
Period 6 — that electron sits far out and is well screened
Lowest ionisation energy of any stable element: 375.7 kJ/mol
examples.ans: It gives up its electron more easily than anything else — largest radius, lowest IE
